title: Regensburg Altstadt: a walk through the medieval core
subtitle: From the Stone Bridge to the palace of Thurn und Taxis, reading the things you would otherwise walk past.
intro: This is a walk through the medieval core of Regensburg, a UNESCO World Heritage site, from the Stone Bridge over the Danube to the palace of Thurn und Taxis at the southern edge of the old town. It is built around things most visitors walk straight past: a Roman gateway, merchant tower houses, a ducal stronghold and the outline of a destroyed synagogue. Where a date or an attribution is disputed, this guide says so rather than pretending certainty.

practical.start: On the Stone Bridge itself, a little out from the south (old town) end, facing south toward the cathedral towers.
practical.end: On Emmeramsplatz in front of Schloss St. Emmeram, at the south of the old town.
practical.terrain: Almost entirely on cobblestones and stone paving, which is uneven. Largely flat, with a gentle rise from the river into the town and a longer flat stretch south to the palace. The outdoor route is mostly step-free and can be followed by wheelchair users, but the cobbles are rough and some lanes are narrow. Several interiors (the Old Town Hall halls, the document Niedermuenster, the Allerheiligenkapelle, the tower houses) involve stairs and are not step-free.
practical.best_time: Morning, for light on the cathedral's west front and fewer people on the bridge. Neupfarrplatz is a working market square, liveliest on weekday mornings. Church and museum interiors keep limited hours, so check before relying on going inside; most exterior stops are visible at any hour.

stops.name: Stone Bridge
stops.stand_here: On the bridge, a little out from the south end, facing south toward the two cathedral spires.
stops.text: You are standing on the oldest largely preserved bridge in Germany, looking south at the old town skyline. The City of Regensburg dates its construction to 1135 to 1146, paid for by the city's merchants with the backing of Duke Heinrich the Proud. It was built as a stone arch bridge of originally 16 arches on 15 piers, about 336 m long. Archaeological work at the southern bridgehead in 2009 concluded it was probably longer still, around 380 m, with long ramps at each end. The first arch was later built over when the Salzstadel went up beside it, which is why you now see fewer arches and about 309 m of bridge. What you are looking at is heavily repaired: the bridge was restored between 2010 and 2018, and stones have been replaced across nine centuries, so treat the surface as modern and the structure beneath as old. The twin cathedral towers ahead, the tallest thing in view, are not medieval to the top: they reach about 105 m and were only finished in 1869.
look_for: the row of visible stone arches
the two cathedral spires to the south
the gate tower at the far end
the tall gabled Salzstadel beside it
stops.next: Walk south off the bridge toward the town. The tall gate tower directly ahead is the Brueckturm; the big gabled warehouse to its left (east) is the Salzstadel. Stop between them.

stops.name: Bridge Tower and Salt Warehouse
stops.stand_here: Between the gate tower and the large warehouse to its east, at the south foot of the bridge.
stops.text: This gate tower is the Brueckturm, the only one of what were once three gate towers on the Stone Bridge to survive. Its dating is not precise: it went up during the building of the medieval town fortifications, somewhere between the middle of the 13th and the middle of the 14th century, so read it as roughly contemporary with the tower houses you will see later. It controlled who entered the free city from Stadtamhof on the far bank. Beside it to the east stands the Salzstadel, the city salt warehouse, built 1616 to 1620 to store salt shipped down the Danube. It is a plain, very large store with a steep roof of five loft floors; the ground floors now hold the free World Heritage visitor centre, a sensible first stop if you want the whole city's history laid out before you walk. Note that both buildings are working survivors rather than reconstructions: the tower is genuinely medieval fabric, the warehouse genuinely 17th century.
look_for: the single surviving gate tower
the steep, many-floored roof of the Salzstadel
the arch cut through for the road
the river behind you
stops.dates: Brueckturm mid-13th to mid-14th century; Salzstadel 1616 to 1620
stops.next: Walk south into Goliathstrasse. Within about 80 m, on your right, a three-storey painting of an armoured giant fills a house wall. Stand across the street from it.

stops.name: Goliath House
stops.stand_here: Across Goliathstrasse from the painted wall, far enough back to see the whole giant.
stops.text: The giant on the wall is Goliath, painted in 1573 by Melchior Bocksberger and repainted several times since, most recently in the 20th century, so the colours are modern even where the composition is old. The house itself is older than its picture: it was built around the middle of the 13th century (usually given as about 1260) on top of the former southern wall of the Roman fort, which is why it sits where it does. Despite the fresco, the name probably does not come from the Bible. The likelier explanation is the Goliards, wandering medieval scholars whose supposed patron was one Golias, after whom an earlier building here may already have been named. Take that as the current best guess rather than a settled fact. From 1290 the house belonged to the Thundorfer patrician family, whose Bishop Leo Thundorfer laid the foundation stone of the present cathedral in 1275. Since 1990 the upper floors have held the Turmtheater. You cannot go in to see the medieval interior, which no longer survives in any case.
look_for: Goliath in full armour leaning on the window frame
David with the sling lower down
the crenellated top of the house
the line where the wall meets the street on the old fort wall
stops.next: Continue a few steps and turn right (southwest) toward Watmarkt. A tall narrow tower house with early Gothic windows stands at Watmarkt 4. Stand at its foot and look up.

stops.name: Baumburger Tower
stops.stand_here: At the foot of the tower on Watmarkt, looking straight up its shaft.
stops.text: This is a Geschlechterturm, one of the tall residential towers that Regensburg's patrician families raised as status symbols. About twenty survive here, the largest concentration north of the Alps, and this one, the Baumburger Turm, is usually called the best preserved. It is about 28 m tall over seven storeys, topped with a ring of battlements. The usual dating is the later 13th century, though you will see figures ranging from about 1250 to about 1270 depending on the source, so treat the exact year as unsettled. It was built by the Ingolstetter family; the Baumburgers, who gave it its name, only acquired it in the 14th century. The ground floor hall once carried a cross-ribbed vault and served as a house chapel. What the towers were for is partly practical (fireproof storage, defence) and partly display: the higher the tower, the higher the family stood. You are looking at private property and cannot go in, but the point is the exterior, and the way it still overtops the roofs around it.
look_for: the battlemented top
the narrow early Gothic windows
how far it rises above neighbouring roofs
the small original window openings
stops.next: Walk west and northwest toward Keplerstrasse, near the river (about 250 m). The Runtingerhaus is at Keplerstrasse 1, a stepped-gable house. Stand before its street front.

stops.name: Runtinger House
stops.stand_here: On Keplerstrasse in front of the stepped-gable façade at number 1.
stops.text: This stepped-gable house is one of the oldest and best preserved patrician houses in the city. Its oldest part, the gabled block on Keplerstrasse, grew out of a house tower of about 1200; the early Gothic house itself dates to the middle of the 13th century, and the building was extended southward around 1330, when the well in the courtyard was dug. In 1367 it passed to the merchant Wilhelm Runtinger and took his name. The Runtingers matter beyond this house: their account book, kept from 1383 to 1407 and now held in the city archive inside this building, is regarded as the most important surviving German merchant's ledger of the Middle Ages, a direct record of long-distance trade to Venice and eastward. After the family, the house served as an inn, was split into small flats in the 19th century, and was restored from around 1960. It now holds the city archive and a medieval hall used for events. The façade in front of you, with its stepped gable and battlement-like top, is the thing to read: a merchant's house built to look like a small fortress.
look_for: the stepped (Staffel) gable
the battlement-like top (Zinnenattika)
arcaded window openings
the passage into the inner courtyard
stops.dates: House tower about 1200; house mid-13th century; extended about 1330; Runtinger from 1367
stops.next: Walk southeast about 120 m to the Rathausplatz. The long building with an off-centre tower and a projecting stone porch is the Old Town Hall. Stand in the square facing the porch.

stops.name: Old Town Hall
stops.stand_here: In Rathausplatz facing the projecting stone entrance porch, with the tall Reichssaal windows to your left.
stops.text: Regensburg was made a Free Imperial City in 1245, and this was its seat of self-government. The complex is of several periods; the great hall behind the tall windows to your left, the Reichssaal, was built after a fire around 1360. Its later fame is political: from 1663 to 1806 the Perpetual Imperial Diet, the standing assembly of the Holy Roman Empire, met in this building, which made a middling-sized city the permanent meeting place of imperial politics for over a century. Below the halls were the courts, the prison and the torture chamber, all part of a working town hall rather than a museum piece. Today the halls and the cells are the document Reichstag museum, entered through the porch in front of you, and are among the few interiors on this walk genuinely worth going inside for. The stone figures guarding the stair to the upper floor are called Schutz and Trutz, protection and defiance. What you see outside is a patchwork of building campaigns from the 13th to the 18th century, not a single design.
look_for: the tall Reichssaal windows and oriel
the projecting stone entrance porch
the two guard figures at the stair
the off-centre tower
stops.dates: Reichssaal after about 1360; Perpetual Diet 1663 to 1806
stops.next: Leave the square heading south into the lanes toward Wahlenstrasse. About 130 m south, a very tall narrow tower rises above the street at Wahlenstrasse 16. Stand below it.

stops.name: Golden Tower
stops.stand_here: Below the tower on Wahlenstrasse, looking up; step back to see it against its neighbours.
stops.text: This is the tallest of the surviving patrician towers, the Goldener Turm, nine storeys wedged into an ordinary row of houses. Its height is quoted two ways and you should know both: the city gives 50 m, while the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns gives 42 m, so the round 50 you will hear on the street is at the upper end of the range. It was built in two phases around 1250 to 1260, the lower storeys first, the upper ones added later, and it belonged to a four-winged town castle named after its owners. Unusually it was also used as a watchtower, which is why, alone among the towers, its upper floors were fitted out rather than left as bare shafts. The name is later: it comes from a tavern that operated here in the 17th century, not from any gilding. The medieval interior is gone, the building having been gutted in the 1890s and rebuilt in the 1950s. It is now a student residence; the open inner courtyard can usually be looked into.
look_for: how far the tower overtops its neighbours
the plain shaft with small windows
the entrance to the inner courtyard
the top storeys, unusually built out
stops.next: Continue south about 130 m to the open Neupfarrplatz. Stand near the free-standing church in the middle of the square, facing it.

stops.name: New Parish Church and the Jewish quarter
stops.stand_here: In the open square near the free-standing church, facing its asymmetric west end.
stops.text: This square sits on top of what was, for more than five centuries, the Jewish quarter of Regensburg, documented from around the year 1000, the earliest recorded Jewish settlement in Germany. It held roughly 39 houses and a synagogue. In February 1519, weeks after the death of the emperor who had protected the community, the city expelled the Jews and demolished the quarter, synagogue included. The church in front of you was begun immediately afterwards, in 1519, on the cleared ground; money ran out in 1528, and when the council turned Protestant in 1542 the unfinished building became the city's first Protestant parish church, which is why it looks truncated. Only part of what was planned was ever built. Excavations across the square from 1995 to 1998 uncovered the cellars of the quarter and, nearby, a hoard of 624 gold coins buried at the end of the 14th century. Some of the excavated cellars can be visited underground as the document Neupfarrplatz. The plain church is worth reading as evidence: a building that marks a destruction.
look_for: the asymmetric, unfinished church
the open market square around it
the paving that covers the excavations
the low white relief nearby
stops.dates: Jewish quarter from about 1000; expulsion and demolition 1519; church begun 1519
stops.next: Walk a few steps west, still on the square, to the low white walk-on relief set into the paving. Stand at its edge.

stops.name: Misrach memorial
stops.stand_here: At the edge of the low white relief in the paving, or on it.
stops.text: This walk-on relief in pale concrete traces, at actual size and on approximately the right spot, the ground plan of the medieval synagogue destroyed in 1519, whose foundations were rediscovered in the excavations here in the 1990s. It was made by the Israeli artist Dani Karavan and inaugurated on 13 July 2005. Its title, Misrach, is Hebrew for east, the direction of prayer, and the Hebrew letters are set into the work. Karavan intended it not only as a memorial but as a place to sit and meet, which is how it is used: people rest on it in the sun and children play between the marked columns. Stand on it and you are standing inside the outline of a building that a mob pulled down. The raised blocks mark the positions of the synagogue's main pillars. It is deliberately low, plain and open, and it is meant to be walked on rather than kept at a distance.
look_for: the outlined ground plan underfoot
the raised blocks marking the pillars
the Hebrew lettering
people sitting on the memorial
stops.next: Leave Neupfarrplatz heading northeast toward the cathedral (about 250 m). Its west front and twin spires are unmistakable. Stand on the Domplatz facing the west front.

stops.name: Saint Peter's Cathedral
stops.stand_here: On Domplatz facing the west front and the two spires.
stops.text: This is the only Gothic cathedral in Bavaria built on the French cathedral model, and the reference building for the whole skyline. Work on the present church began after fires destroyed its predecessor: sources give 1273 for the fire and 1275 for the start of the new building, and construction then ran, on and off, into the 16th century. Here is the thing most guides gloss over: the two openwork spires in front of you are not medieval. The cathedral stood for over 350 years with stunted tower stumps. The spires were built only from 1859 to 1869 under King Ludwig I, and the transept gables completed by 1872, in a careful neo-Gothic that matches the old work closely. They rise about 105 m. So when you photograph the classic view, the silhouette is largely a 19th century creation on a 13th to 16th century body. Inside (free to enter) are one of the largest surviving sets of medieval stained glass in the German-speaking lands, from the 13th and 14th centuries. To the left of the west front, a plainer older tower, the Eselsturm, survives from the Romanesque predecessor.
look_for: the two openwork spires (19th century)
the older plain tower to the left (Eselsturm)
the sculpted west portal
the green sandstone of the upper work
stops.dates: Begun 1273 to 1275; spires 1859 to 1869; about 105 m
stops.next: Walk around the north (left) side of the cathedral to the small square Unter den Schwiboegen. A blocky stone arch is embedded among the houses. Stand before it.

stops.name: Porta Praetoria
stops.stand_here: In the lane Unter den Schwiboegen, facing the heavy stone arch set into the houses.
stops.text: This heavy stone arch is the north gate of the Roman fortress Castra Regina, whose legionary garrison was established here in AD 179 under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, the founding date of the city. Together with the Porta Nigra in Trier it is one of only two Roman gates still partly standing north of the Alps. What survives is a fragment: one archway and part of a flanking tower, built of large limestone blocks and later swallowed by the medieval and modern houses around it, which is why you meet it in a corner rather than in the open. Its Roman identity was only recognised in the 19th century. Look at the size and rough fit of the lowest blocks against the smaller stonework above and you can read the join between Roman work and everything built on top of it later. The gate faced the rivers, toward the country beyond the Danube. It is out in the street and free to look at at any hour.
look_for: the large rough Roman limestone blocks
the single surviving arch
the medieval and later houses built onto it
the smaller stonework above the Roman base
stops.next: Go to the cathedral cloister behind the church; the Allerheiligenkapelle stands in the cloister (access via the cathedral or on a guided visit). Position yourself where you can see the small central-plan chapel, or read this at the cloister entrance.

stops.name: All Saints' Chapel
stops.stand_here: In the cathedral cloister, or at its entrance, where you can see the small square chapel with an octagonal upper storey.
stops.text: Behind the cathedral, in the double cloister, stands a small square chapel with an octagonal upper storey: the Allerheiligenkapelle, one of the finest pieces of Romanesque architecture in Bavaria and easy to walk past without noticing. It was built around 1160 as the burial chapel of Bishop Hartwig II, who died in 1164 and who, unusually, chose not to be buried at St Emmeram like earlier bishops but in his own chapel in the middle of the cathedral precinct. It is generally attributed to Comacine masters, builders from northern Italy, and its plan and proportions recall Lombard and Ravennate models. Inside are wall paintings of the Apocalypse from the building period, though they have been heavily altered by restoration, so what survives is partly original design and partly later hand. Note that the chapel is often closed for conservation reasons and is normally seen only on a guided cloister visit, so treat this stop as something to locate and understand rather than necessarily to enter. Even from outside, the tiered square-then-octagon form is the thing to read.
look_for: the square base with an octagonal upper storey
the cloister arcades around it
small round-arched Romanesque windows
the plain, tiered mass of the building
stops.next: Leave the cloister area for the west side of the Alter Kornmarkt, the large square southeast of the cathedral. A massive blocky tower stands at Domstrasse 3, linked to a neighbouring house by an arch over the street. Stand at its foot.

stops.name: Roman Tower (Herzogsturm)
stops.stand_here: At the foot of the massive tower at Domstrasse 3 on the Alter Kornmarkt, near the arch that spans the street.
stops.text: This massive block goes by three names: Roemerturm is the usual one, Herzogsturm and Heidenturm are the others, and the confusion is worth a moment because it tells you what the tower is. It belonged to the ducal palace, not to a merchant family, so it is not one of the patrician status towers you saw earlier. It stands about 28 m high on a roughly 14 by 14 m plan, with lower walls over 4 m thick, and it was linked to the neighbouring Herzogshof by an arch over the street (the present arch is a 20th century replacement of one removed in 1855). The lowest part, of large rusticated blocks reusing Roman stone, is the reason for the Roman name; it is dated only loosely, from post-Carolingian to Hohenstaufen times, and has never been pinned to an exact year. The upper storeys are plainer 14th century rubble work. It served as the stronghold of the palace, effectively a strongroom and refuge. Read the change in masonry from bottom to top: it is a tower built and heightened in stages over centuries.
look_for: the huge rusticated lower blocks
the arch linking it to the neighbouring house
the change in masonry higher up
the sheer wall thickness at the door
stops.dates: Base post-Carolingian to Hohenstaufen; upper storeys 14th century
stops.next: Cross the Alter Kornmarkt to the east side, to the Niedermuenster church. The entrance to the underground document Niedermuenster is by the church (guided visits only). Stand by the church.

stops.name: document Niedermuenster (excavation)
stops.stand_here: By the Niedermuenster church on the Alter Kornmarkt, near the entrance used for guided visits.
stops.text: Under the Romanesque Niedermuenster church here lies one of the largest church excavations in Germany, dug between 1963 and 1969 when underfloor heating was being installed, opening up around 600 m2 of stacked history up to 5 m deep. It is called the document Niedermuenster and can be seen only on a guided visit, so from up here you are standing on top of it rather than in it. What is below, in order downward, runs from the 10th century church of the noble women's convent, through an early monumental palace chapel of the 7th century, down to the barrack foundations of the Roman legionary fort in the northeast corner of Castra Regina. It holds the graves of the Bavarian duke Heinrich I and his wife Judith, and the grave of Saint Erhard, a wandering bishop buried here after around 700 and canonised in 1052, whose grave stayed in place through every rebuilding of the church above. It is, in effect, a vertical section through 2,000 years of the city, which is why it is worth booking a guided descent.
look_for: the Romanesque church above the site
the entrance used for guided visits
the Alter Kornmarkt around you
notices with visiting times
stops.dates: Excavated 1963 to 1969; layers from the 2nd to the 12th century
stops.next: Walk south out of the old core, about 700 m, down toward Emmeramsplatz. The large palace complex at the south end of the old town is Schloss St. Emmeram. Stand on Emmeramsplatz facing the entrance.

stops.name: St. Emmeram Palace
stops.stand_here: On Emmeramsplatz facing the palace entrance, with the basilica tower to your right.
stops.text: This large complex is where the walk ends and where the city's oldest institution and one of its newer owners meet. It began as the Benedictine abbey of St Emmeram, founded around 739 at the grave of the itinerant Frankish bishop Emmeram, and was for a thousand years one of the most important monasteries in southern Germany. The abbey church beside the palace, now the basilica of St Emmeram, keeps genuinely old fabric, including 11th century work and stone reliefs by the north portal that are among the earliest of their kind in Germany; its interior was given a full Baroque refurbishment by the Asam brothers between 1731 and 1733. The monastery was dissolved in the secularisation of 1803, and in compensation for giving up their imperial postal rights the princely house of Thurn und Taxis took over the buildings, converting them from 1812 into their residence. Much of the palace you see is therefore a 19th century rebuilding of a much older abbey, and the family still lives in part of it, so only sections and the Romanesque cloister are open, on tickets. Treat the ensemble as layered: an 8th century foundation, a Baroque church, a 19th century palace.
look_for: the long palace frontage
the tower of the basilica
the entrance to the museums and cloister
the scale of the complex at the town's south edge
stops.dates: Abbey founded about 739; basilica Baroque work 1731 to 1733; palace from 1812
stops.next: End of walk. The Emmeramsplatz and Fuerstliche Schatzkammer are here; the main station is a short walk south.
